extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science; scientists interested in foundations/method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates conceptual standards about causation, necessity, routine in perception, and probability as presented in a philosophy-of-science textbook chapter. Focuses on criteria scientists and philosophers use to justify inference from past experience to future expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definition of cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a sequence of perceptions D, E, F, G is invariably preceded by the perception C, or the perceptions C, D, E, F, G always occur in this order (i.e., form a routine of experience), C is said to be a cause of D, E, F, G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No phenomenon has only one cause; all antecedent stages are successive causes. Science, when stating causes, is really describing successive stages of a routine of experience. John Stuart Mill's phrase 'uniform antecedence' captures this scientific concept of causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Width of the term 'cause'
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific sense of 'cause' is elastic: causes of an individual thing may be widened into a description of many prior conditions (e.g., causes of an ash-tree's growth include garden, metropolis, soil, geology, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing all causes of an individual object leads to the unmanageable history of the universe; science therefore typically traces one line or range of causes at a time and deals with general classes (e.g., 'ash-trees' or 'trees in general') rather than the total causes of a single individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fetishizing 'force' as explanatory
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'force' often symbolizes metaphysical obscurity; talking of 'forces' (mechanical, vital, social) frequently hides rather than adds knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences relevant to scientific explanation are reducible to motions or changes; describing motions (e.g., chemical processes, radiation) is legitimate, but invoking 'forces' as an explanatory ultimate introduces a 'mountain of obscurity.' All cause, in science, is routine (concise description) rather than an account of 'why' in a metaphysical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity belongs to conceptions, not perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical necessity arises from definitions and axioms in the world of conceptions (e.g., geometry, theory of gravitation) and does not exist inherently in sequences of sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mental theory of planetary motion or circle geometry has logical necessity, but transferring that necessity to the actual sequence of perceptions (observed planetary positions) is illegitimate; predictable description and conceptual necessity differ from invariable necessity in perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine in perception is a necessary condition of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition or routine (invariable order of perceptions) is essential for thought; the law that 'the same set of causes is always accompanied by the same effect' underpins the possibility of prediction and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sequences of perceptions did not repeat (if outcomes after antecedents were random), knowledge and reasoning would be impossible. Routine is a product (plausibly) of the perceptive faculty evolved to guide conduct and survival; attacks on the belief in routine (e.g., reported miracles) undermine the basis of practical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable and provable (proof in perceptions = probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty (proof) applies only to conceptions; in the field of perceptions, 'proof' ultimately equates to probability because inferences about perceptions rest on the assumed routine of past experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etymology links 'probable' and 'provable.' Using 'prove' about perceptual phenomena involves inferring routine from past repetition. Examples (Sir William Thomson) show scientists using 'prove' to mean strong probabilistic inference grounded in past experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's rule for probability of recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event has happened p times and failed q times, the probability that it will happen next is (p+1)/(p+q+1) (odds = (p+1)/(q+1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to scientific claims: frequent past repetition across individuals and classes yields overwhelming odds that a newly observed phenomenon follows routine. Examples: sun rising (practical certainty), single careful experiment (far less certainty). Laplace's theorem formalizes how past frequency affects belief about future recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of miracles/anomalies by probabilistic weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Given extreme rarity of well-authenticated breaches of routine in past experience, the odds against a 'miracle' occurring in the next sequence of perceptions are astronomically large (practically making miracles 'incredible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even giving generous allowance to reported miracles, Laplace's formula yields odds (e.g., about 1,000 million to 1) against recurrence; therefore belief in miracles should not guide practical conduct. The word 'proved' is used in the probabilistic sense applicable to perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior ignorance and the basis of Laplace's theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace's probabilistic conclusions depend on assumptions about prior ignorance; one cannot justly assume routines and anomalies are equally likely without experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: bag with white (routine) and black (anomy) balls — assuming equal numbers without evidence is unjustified. The appropriate probability distribution must be informed by experience; priors matter and must be chosen with regard to what is known (i.e., update beliefs from experience rather than assume equiprobability).
